Apparent Compression, Real Stability:
The Intrinsic Dimension of Learning a Quantum Wavefunction

Lu Wei Affiliation: Data Science Department Email: luw744895@gmail.com    Yufeng Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University Email: yufeng.wang.2@stonybrook.edu    Chenfeng Cao Affiliation: Dahlem Center for Complex Quantum Systems, Freie Universität Berlin Email: chenfeng.cao@fu-berlin.de    Haibin Ling Affiliation: Westlake University Email: linghaibin@westlake.edu.cn
Abstract

How many directions in weight space does training need? The intrinsic dimension answers this with the smallest number of random directions in which training still reaches a target accuracy, and small values have motivated parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA. We measure it for variational Monte Carlo (VMC), which trains a neural network to represent the ground state of a quantum many-body system. VMC is a demanding test, because the network generates its own training samples and every gradient is noisy, and a revealing one, because the exact answer is known and every run can be scored. We train only a small latent vector that a frozen random map turns into the network’s weights, with no change to the standard natural-gradient optimizer. We find that a small dimension can be misleading, while the stability it brings is real. On a magnet with a hard sign pattern, a network that cannot represent signs reaches its best energy in 8 of 28,642 directions, but only because no such network can go lower; once signs are learnable, neither the signs nor the magnitudes are cheap. The dimension rises across a quantum phase transition, so it tracks how difficult a state is at far less compute than fitting a scaling law, yet it never falls below a floor set by the random subspace itself, even where the ground state is nearly trivial. Training in the subspace, in contrast, never diverged in our experiments, whereas full-parameter training with the same settings did, and a control with matched solvers attributes the difference to the reduced dimension.

1 Introduction

How many directions in weight space does training need? Li et al. (2018) answered this question by training a network only inside a random low-dimensional subspace of its weights and recording the smallest subspace dimension at which training still reaches 90% of the full model’s performance. They called this number the intrinsic dimension of the objective landscape, and measured it for supervised and reinforcement learning. Later work measured it for the fine-tuning of language models (Aghajanyan et al., 2021), where it motivates parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022).

This paper brings the measurement to variational Monte Carlo (VMC), the standard way to train a neural network to represent the ground state of a quantum many-body system (Carleo & Troyer, 2017). Such a network, called a neural quantum state (NQS), assigns to every configuration of the system an amplitude with a magnitude and a sign, and VMC adjusts its weights to lower the energy of the state it represents. The setting differs from the ones above in three ways. First, there is no dataset. The energy and its gradient are estimated from configurations sampled from the network itself, so every gradient is noisy and the noise depends on the current weights. Second, training uses a natural-gradient method called stochastic reconfiguration (Sorella, 1998; Sorella, 2001, SR;), rather than plain gradient descent. Third, for the systems we study the exact ground-state energy is known, so the error of every run can be computed exactly, which benchmarks in vision, language and control do not offer. To our knowledge no published work measures intrinsic dimension in this setting. It is not obvious in advance that training in a random subspace survives the sampling noise, or what the measured number would mean.

We restrict VMC training to a random subspace as follows (Fig. 1). A map gg is drawn at random and then frozen. It generates all PP weights of the network from a latent vector zz of dimension d≪Pd\ll P, and only zz is trained, so training moves within a random dd-dimensional slice of weight space. SR applies to zz with no change to the training loop, because the natural-gradient metric of zz follows from that of the weights by the chain rule (Sec. 3.3). We then define d∗d^{*} as the smallest dd at which the median relative energy error over random seeds falls below a threshold τ\tau within a fixed training budget. It is the counterpart, at a fixed budget, of the intrinsic dimension of (Li et al., 2018).

We measure d∗d^{*} on two spin models. The first is a frustrated Heisenberg magnet, where the pattern of signs of the ground state is widely regarded as the hard part to learn (Westerhout et al., 2020; Schurov et al., 2025). The second is the transverse-field Ising chain, whose ground state has no signs and which undergoes a quantum phase transition. Besides the linear map of Li et al. (2018) we test a nonlinear map modelled on Mapping Networks (Sen & Mukherjee, 2026). It trails the linear map on the frustrated magnet and is comparable on the Ising chain (Secs. 4.1, 4.3).

We propose no new training algorithm. Instead, our main contributions are a measurement and three findings that it yields.

  • •

    Intrinsic-dimension measurement for VMC. We restrict the training of a neural quantum state to a random subspace and show that SR applies without modification, so the measurement can be added to an existing VMC code as is. Every run is scored against an exact ground-state energy (Sec. 3).

  • •

    Subspace training is robust under gradient noise. In all 246 subspace runs of our sign-structure study, at two lattice sizes, training never diverged, while full-parameter training with the same optimizer settings diverged 41 times in 35 runs at the larger size. A control that reruns the subspace with the full-parameter solver attributes the gap to the dimension. The subspace removes divergence. It does not remove the dependence of the final energy on the random seed (Secs. 4.1, 4.4).

  • •

    Apparent compression can be a variational bound. On the frustrated magnet, a network with non-negative amplitudes reaches its best energy in 8 of 28,642 random directions. That energy is the lowest that any non-negative wavefunction can reach, so the small d∗d^{*} is a property of the model class and says nothing about the ground state. In a model that can represent signs, we give the sign and the amplitude parameters separate budgets and compare with a control that has the exact sign built in. Neither part is cheap. The error keeps falling as amplitude dimensions are added, up to the largest subspace we train, and once the amplitude is resolved the sign needs its whole block of parameters. With every parameter trainable, a learned sign still costs 9×9\times in error against an exact one at equal steps (Sec. 4.2). The same protocol applies to any method that divides a budget of trainable dimensions among parameter blocks, such as low-rank adaptation (Sec. 5.1).

  • •

    The measured dimension tracks a phase transition, above a floor set by the random slice. On the Ising chain, d∗d^{*} rises about 4×4\times across the transition at two system sizes, at a threshold for which we verify that d∗d^{*} does not change when the training budget is tripled. Deep in the paramagnet d∗d^{*} falls only to 64, although the ground state there is nearly a product state. Part of d∗d^{*} is therefore a cost of the random slice itself (Sec. 4.3).

2 Related work

Intrinsic dimension and parameter-efficient training. Li et al. (2018) measured intrinsic dimension on supervised vision tasks and, with DQN and evolution strategies, on control and Atari tasks. Aghajanyan et al. (2021) measured it for the fine-tuning of pretrained language models, where 200 parameters projected back into the full space bring RoBERTa to 90% of full fine-tuning performance on MRPC. LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) builds a method on this low dimension. It freezes the pretrained weights, trains a low-rank update in each layer, and needs 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B. For supervised networks, the threshold dimension of a random affine subspace rises as the target loss falls and falls as the initial loss falls (Larsen et al., 2022). Our d∗d^{*} is likewise defined at a fixed threshold τ\tau and a fixed initialization θ0\theta_{0}. The lottery-ticket hypothesis (Frankle & Carbin, 2019) makes a related claim in a different basis, a small sub-network found by search, in place of a small random subspace that involves no search. Our work returns to the measurement. In VMC the objective can only be sampled, as in the control and Atari tasks, but exact ground truth allows two controls that those tasks do not offer. An exact-sign control separates the amplitude from the sign, and a product-state limit exposes the floor set by the random slice.

Weight generation through fixed maps. Mapping Networks (Sen & Mukherjee, 2026) are a nonlinear counterpart of the linear subspace. They generate all weights from a latent vector through a frozen orthogonal map that the latent modulates, followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and they train with auxiliary stability, smoothness and alignment losses. In quantum tomography, HyperRBMs instead let a hypernetwork modulate the biases of a restricted Boltzmann machine as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter (Tonner et al., 2026). Neither work measures the smallest trainable dimension, which is what we study.

NQS optimization. Neural quantum states were introduced by Carleo & Troyer (2017). Our base ansatz is an autoregressive NQS (Sharir et al., 2020). VMC training is preconditioned by SR (Sorella, 1998; Sorella, 2001), whose metric is the quantum geometric tensor (Stokes et al., 2020; Vicentini et al., 2022), and minSR (Chen & Heyl, 2024) and an exact sample-space form of SR (Rende et al., 2024b) make it affordable at large parameter counts. Parameter-efficient training is also used for NQS. Fine-tuning only the output layer transfers a pretrained NQS across couplings (Rende et al., 2024a). Closest to our study, Rende et al. (2026) fit compute scaling laws for NQS and assign each Hamiltonian a compute exponent, at a cost of ∼105{\sim}10^{5} A100 GPU-hours.

Sign structure as the hard part. Recent work points to the sign, or phase, of the wavefunction as the hard part from two directions. In complex-valued NQS the phase-gradient estimator can be the bottleneck of training, which low-variance estimators relieve (Xue et al., 2026). The learning complexity of many-body sign structures has been analyzed with Boolean Fourier analysis on exact ground states (Schurov et al., 2025). Given the exact signs of the same model at 6×66\times 6, Bukov et al. (2021) still did not reach a more accurate state. Our dissection measures the same cost inside VMC training, both in dimensions and in optimization. Döschl & Bohrdt (2026) study the interpretability of NQS, whereas we study their trainable dimension.

Machine-learning probes of phase transitions. The intrinsic dimension of the data, measured on Monte Carlo spin configurations, has a minimum with universal finite-size scaling at continuous transitions (Mendes-Santos et al., 2021). We measure the intrinsic dimension of training instead, and find a rise across the transition that relaxes deep in the paramagnet to a floor set by the random slice (Sec. 4.3). The two quantities behave in opposite ways at the transition, so they describe different geometries. Weight-space analyses detect phase transitions in the weights of trained NQS (Hernandes et al., 2025). d∗d^{*} constrains the training itself, so the two approaches are complementary.

3 Method: Subspace-Restricted VMC

Our method, i.e., subspace-restricted VMC, offers three reusable pieces: a measurement of intrinsic dimension for an objective that can only be sampled (Sec. 3.3), a budget protocol that tells a block with too few dimensions from one that is hard to learn (Sec. 4.2), and a health guard for latent training (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Setup and notation

Let θ∈ℝP\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{P} be the full weight vector of a base NQS ansatz with PP parameters, and ψθ​(σ)\psi_{\theta}(\sigma) the (unnormalized) wavefunction amplitude it assigns to spin configuration σ\sigma. Training minimizes the variational energy E=⟨ψθ|H|ψθ⟩/⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩E=\langle\psi_{\theta}|H|\psi_{\theta}\rangle/\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle of a Hamiltonian HH, estimated by Monte Carlo sampling from |ψθ|2|\psi_{\theta}|^{2} with error-of-mean σE\sigma_{E}. With E0E_{0} the exact ground-state energy, accuracy is the relative error εrel=(E−E0)/|E0|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}=(E-E_{0})/|E_{0}|. We write ε\varepsilon for εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} where unambiguous. Subspace restriction trains only a latent z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d≪Pd\ll P, through a frozen map gg with θ=g⁡(z)\theta=g(z) (Fig. 1a). We write λ\lambda for the generic Hamiltonian coupling being scanned.

The base ansatz is an autoregressive neural network (ARNN) wavefunction ψθ\psi_{\theta} (Sharir et al., 2020). Normalization and lattice symmetry are built into its architecture, so a frozen weight map cannot break them and no constraint on the weights is needed. We study two systems.

  • •

    Frustrated testbed. The 2D J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model has nearest-neighbor coupling J1J_{1} and next-nearest-neighbor coupling J2J_{2}, and its frustration is tuned by J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. We use a 4×44\times 4 periodic lattice at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, where exact diagonalization gives E0=−8.4579233514E_{0}=-8.4579233514 and the network has P=28,642P=28{,}642 parameters. A 6×66\times 6 extension appears in Secs. 4.2 and 4.4.

  • •

    Sign-free testbed. The transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) is an Ising spin chain with coupling JJ and transverse magnetic field hh, and it has a quantum phase transition at h/J=1h/J=1. We use chain lengths L=16L=16 and L=24L=24. In Sec. 3.3 the symbol JJ denotes a Jacobian, and the TFIM coupling appears only in the ratio h/Jh/J.

3.2 Four training configurations

We compare four training configurations, named TC1 to TC4, as summarized in Table 1. All four start from the same initialization θ0\theta_{0} of the same ansatz and use the same training loop and sampler. They differ in which coordinates are trainable. TC1 trains all PP parameters and is the reference. TC2 trains dd coordinates of a random linear subspace through θ0\theta_{0}, a per-group variant of the construction of Li et al. (2018), and is the primary instrument. TC3 trains dd coordinates through the same map followed by a tanh, our variant of the Mapping Networks construction. TC4 trains only the last parameter group and freezes the rest, a control that asks whether a fixed, cheap restriction already suffices. Comparisons are made at equal step counts, and between TC2 and TC3 at matched dd.

Config. Construction Trainable dim. Role
TC1 full θ\theta PP full-parameter reference (minSR)
TC2 θk=θ0,k+sk​Wk​zk\theta_{k}=\theta_{0,k}+s_{k}\,W_{k}z_{k} dd linear subspace (Li et al.)
TC3 θk=θ0,k+sk​tanh⁡(Wk​zk)\theta_{k}=\theta_{0,k}+s_{k}\tanh(W_{k}z_{k}) dd nonlinear mapping (tanh variant)
TC4 last parameter group :=z:=z, rest frozen at θ0\theta_{0} last-group size cheap-subspace control

The construction shared by TC2 and TC3 works per group, over the ansatz’s top-level parameter groups indexed by kk. Here θ0\theta_{0} is the standard initialization, with θ0,k\theta_{0,k} its group-kk block. The matrix WkW_{k} is frozen and has orthonormal columns, from the QR decomposition of a seeded Gaussian. The block zkz_{k} is the part of the latent allocated to group kk. The scale sk=std⁡(θ0,k)s_{k}=\mathrm{std}(\theta_{0,k}) keeps generated perturbations at that group’s natural initialization scale.

TC3 differs from the published Mapping Networks construction (Sen & Mukherjee, 2026). We omit their latent-driven weight modulation and their auxiliary stability/smoothness/alignment losses, training the latent against the energy alone. In their image-classification ablation the unmodulated variant trails the full method by 2–4%, so TC3, which omits the auxiliary losses as well, likely understates what the full construction could reach. The latent budget dd is split across parameter groups in proportion to group size, with a minimum of 1 and a cap at the group size. We write deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} for the realized total. The effective map seed is the map seed plus the run seed, so different seeds also randomize the frozen map, as in the repeated runs of (Li et al., 2018).

3.3 Stochastic reconfiguration in the latent space

SR needs the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) SθS_{\theta}, the Gram matrix of the log-derivatives ∂θlog⁡ψθ\partial_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}. Because zz is the only trainable collection, automatic differentiation yields log-derivatives directly in zz-space, and SR operates with the pullback

Sz=J†​Sθ​J,J=∂θ∂z,S_{z}=J^{\dagger}S_{\theta}J,\qquad J=\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial z}, (1)

where JJ is the Jacobian of the frozen map. The training driver, the VMC loop of NetKet (Carleo et al., 2019; Vicentini et al., 2022), is unchanged. The natural-gradient geometry of VMC is therefore automatically the correct geometry of the latent space. The implementation is uniform across configurations. We use plain SGD under SR, with no adaptive optimizer stacked on the preconditioner. SR uses a dense QGT, an explicit d×dd\times d tensor, for every trainable dimension ≤4096\leq 4096, that is, for TC2 to TC4, and minSR for TC1. We control for that split by rerunning TC2 at 6×66\times 6 and d=3072d=3072 on minSR, with 21 runs over all seven couplings at a median of 1120 steps. These runs also log zero divergence events, so the stability contrast survives solver matching.

3.4 Health protocol for noisy-objective training

Divergence events are counted, logged, and reported as part of the result. An event is declared when the Monte Carlo energy estimate is not finite, jumps upward, or violates the variational floor, that is, falls below the exact energy E0E_{0} by more than the sampling noise allows. On an event we roll back to the best variables, halve the learning rate and rebuild the driver, and we abort after a maximum number of resets.

The floor guard is necessary when the objective is noisy. Detectors that only catch NaNs and upward jumps, which is the standard pattern in the field, miss corruption of the estimator in the downward direction, which a frozen map can amplify. Health-aware monitoring of training trajectories is also emerging in NQS practice (Wang et al., 2026). The thresholds, and an incident that only the floor guard catches, are in Appendix B.

3.5 The observable

The observable is the smallest dd at which the median error over seeds meets a threshold:

d∗​(λ,τ):=min⁡{d:medianseeds​εrel​(d,λ)≤τ}d^{*}(\lambda;\tau):=\min\{\,d\ :\ \mathrm{median}_{\text{seeds}}\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}(d,\lambda)\leq\tau\,\} (2)

at coupling λ\lambda and accuracy threshold τ\tau, under a fixed budget of steps or compute per run (Fig. 1b). The median over seeds is essential, because the orientation of the random subspace selects among distinct attractors (Sec. 4.1), so values from a single seed are not stable. As defined, d∗d^{*} depends on the budget. Sec. 4.3 shows at which threshold it becomes independent of the budget in practice.

4 Experiments

4.1 Subspace training survives gradient noise

Setup. We run the 4×44\times 4 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model at the maximally frustrated coupling J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, on the latent grid d∈{8,32,128,512}d\in\{8,32,128,512\}, with 3 seeds per cell. Every configuration is compared within the first 880 steps, the number TC1 completed.

Stability under gradient noise. All 9 runs of TC3 at d≥32d\geq 32 finished with no divergence event and no abort, and there were zero divergence events across all 24 latent-subspace (TC2/TC3) runs. Latent-only optimization under intrinsic gradient noise is viable, and Sec. 4.4 shows it is more stable than full-parameter training at scale.

A shared bound. Every high-capacity configuration converges to the same εrel≈0.5271\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\approx 0.5271 (Table 2): full TC1, last-layer TC4 (deff=578d_{\mathrm{eff}}=578), and TC2 with best seeds down to d=8d=8. That is E=−3.99975E=-3.99975, within 0.006%0.006\% of the smallest diagonal element of HH, −4-4, attained by the classical Néel and stripe configurations. This value does not depend on the network. Every off-diagonal element of HH in this basis is non-negative, so no wavefunction with non-negative amplitudes can go below that diagonal minimum, and any amplitude function concentrated on those configurations attains it. We call it the positive-cone bound. Reaching it in d=8d=8 of P=28,642P=28{,}642 dimensions, an apparent 3,500×3{,}500\times compression, therefore says nothing about the amplitudes of the ground state. Section 4.2 removes the bound with an exact-sign control.

The nonlinear map. TC3 is dominated by TC2 at every matched dd and is far slower to converge at d=8d=8 (median ε=1.46\varepsilon=1.46 within 880 steps, Fig. 5). The nonlinear construction therefore underperforms on the frustrated system, whose sign-free optimum is a set of classical configurations. On the TFIM it is roughly on par with the linear subspace (Appendix D). We tested one nonlinear construction, a tanh variant of the mapping of Sen & Mukherjee (2026) trained with the task loss only, without their weight modulation or auxiliary losses, and in one architecture family. Our statements about the nonlinear map are limited to this variant.

Seed dependence and conditioning. The seeds of TC2 are bimodal. They end at ε≈0.527\varepsilon\approx 0.527 or at 0.6460.646, that is, at E≈−4E\approx-4 or −3-3, which are both energies of classical Ising configurations. The orientation of the random subspace selects the basin, which is why d∗d^{*} is defined by a median over seeds. At d=512d=512 all six runs reach the lower attractor (Appendix D). The condition number of the QGT in zz-space does not predict the quality of the optimization. TC2 wins with a condition number of about 101010^{10}, and TC3 loses with 10210^{2} to 10410^{4}. The conditioning of the curvature is therefore a poor proxy for quality here.

4.2 An exact-sign control separates amplitude from sign

This subsection asks where the difficulty of the ground state lies, in the amplitude or in the sign. Section 4.1 measured d∗d^{*} against the positive-cone bound. To get below the bound the model must represent signs, so we extend the same ansatz with a small phase network, log⁡ψ=log⁡|ψ|+i​ϕ​(σ)\log\psi=\log|\psi|+i\phi(\sigma). Here ϕ\phi is a 2-layer tanh MLP. It holds 1,633 of the Pc=30,275P_{c}=30{,}275 real parameters of the extended model (5.4%). We call these parameters the sign block and the rest the amplitude block. All runs use the same coupling (4×44\times 4, J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5) and 3 seeds per cell, and they log 0 divergence events.

Full-parameter reference. Configurations on the sign-capable model carry the suffix c. Full-parameter training of the extended model, TC1c, reaches a median best ε\varepsilon of 0.0444 (seeds 0.0382, 0.0444 and 0.1920), which is 12×12\times below the bound. It does so in only ∼600{\sim}600 steps.

Proportional allocation fails. The random-subspace construction that reaches the bound of Sec. 4.1 at d=8d=8 stays far from the sign-capable reference. The medians of TC2c are 0.690, 0.482, 0.395 and 0.316 at d=8d=8, 32, 128 and 512, against the pre-registered gate of 2×2\timesTC1c =0.0888=0.0888, even though these runs take 1,420–2,040 steps against the 600 of the reference. This failure has two possible causes. Proportional allocation assigns latent dimensions by group size, so the phase network receives only ∼28{\sim}28 of 512 dimensions, and the sign block may simply have too few dimensions. Alternatively, the sign structure itself may need many dimensions. Reallocating within one budget cannot separate the two, because every dimension moved into the sign block leaves the amplitude block. We therefore hold one block fixed and sweep the other, and add an exact-sign control on the amplitude side.

The exact-sign control. We freeze the exact sign of the ground state, taken from exact diagonalization, into the amplitude network, logψ=log|ψθ|+iπ[s0(σ)<0]\log\psi=\log|\psi_{\theta}|+i\pi\,[s_{0}(\sigma)<0]. Every trainable direction is then an amplitude direction, and the target is the true ground state. The sign is a lookup table and adds no parameters. Each run takes 1,500 steps, with 3 seeds and the same sampler and optimizer. The amplitude is not cheap. The median εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} falls smoothly from 0.37 at d=8d=8 to 0.052 at d=512d=512 and 0.031 at d=2048d=2048, while the full amplitude network reaches 2.6×10−32.6\times 10^{-3} (Fig. 2a). The d=8d=8 cells have converged, with the best εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} within 3.1% over their last 300 steps, so the 3,500×3{,}500\times of Sec. 4.1 does not survive once the bound is removed. No subspace up to d=2048d=2048 reaches 10−210^{-2}.

Amplitude swept, sign block complete. With all 1,633 dimensions of the sign block trainable, the error falls from 0.42 at 2 amplitude dimensions to 0.053 at 415 and 0.039 at 1,024 (Fig. 2a, and Table 5 in the appendix). From 415 dimensions on it matches the exact-sign control within 6%. At 2 and 8 it does better than the exact sign, which need not be the best sign for a restricted amplitude.

Sign swept, amplitude fixed. With the amplitude fixed at 1,024 dimensions, the median error at 402 of the 1,633 sign dimensions is 1.24×1.24\times that of the complete block. At 128 it is 2.4×2.4\times and at 32 it is 7.3×7.3\times (Fig. 2b). At this amplitude dimension the seed ranges at 402 and 1,633 sign dimensions overlap (0.044–0.050 against 0.038–0.046). At 415 amplitude dimensions they separate (0.060–0.067 against 0.050–0.055, a ratio of 1.18×1.18\times). Once the amplitude is resolved, the sign therefore needs its whole block. The full grid (Fig. 7 in the appendix) shows that this demand appears only then. With 2–128 amplitude dimensions, a 402-dimensional sign block comes within 1.1×1.1\times of the complete one (0.730.73–1.07×1.07\times). Proportional allocation leaves the sign block 28 dimensions, and it sits 5.9×5.9\times above the exact-sign control at the same 484 amplitude dimensions, both within 1,420 steps.

The cost of the sign in optimization. With every parameter trainable, the sign-capable model reaches a median εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} of 0.044 in its first 600 steps, against 4.9×10−34.9\times 10^{-3} for the same amplitude network given the exact sign. This is a factor of 9 at equal steps under the same minSR solver. It fits an analysis of estimator variance in which the phase gradient can bottleneck the training of complex-valued NQS (Xue et al., 2026).

Dependence on frustration. We scan the frustration J2/J1∈{0.40,0.45,…,0.70}J_{2}/J_{1}\in\{0.40,0.45,\ldots,0.70\} at fixed dd, at both lattice sizes (Table 4 and Fig. 6 in Appendix E). The error follows the phase structure of the model. At 4×44\times 4, at d=128d=128 and d=512d=512, every coupling with J2/J1≤0.55J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.55 has a higher error than every coupling with J2/J1≥0.60J_{2}/J_{1}\geq 0.60, and at 6×66\times 6 the error at d=3072d=3072 peaks at J2/J1=0.55J_{2}/J_{1}=0.55.

The saturated allocation at 6×66\times 6. At 6×66\times 6 the allocation d=3072d=3072 gives the sign block all of its 2,273 dimensions and the amplitude the remaining 799. Its median per coupling still stays 3.83.8–7.7×7.7\times above the best full-parameter seed. We gate on the best seed here and ask the median to come within 2×2\times of it, which we call the robust gate (Sec. 4.4). Under this gate dc∗d^{*}_{c}, the smallest dd that passes the gate, is right-censored (>3072>3072) at every coupling. The sign block is fully covered while the amplitude has only 799 of 28,642 dimensions, so the two deficits cannot be separated here. We report a joint failure of the saturated budget (Appendix A).

4.3 d∗d^{*} tracks the phase transition, above a floor set by the random slice

This subsection asks what the measured dimension responds to. We measure d∗d^{*} across a quantum phase transition, where the structure of the ground state changes, and in a limit where the ground state is nearly trivial.

Setup. We use TFIM chains. Their ground states have no signs, so the real-amplitude ARNN is adequate and small thresholds are meaningful. The linear subspace (TC2) is the primary configuration. We use three protocols and never mix them. The base protocol uses L=16L=16, a fixed budget of 2000 steps and d∈{2,…,128}d\in\{2,\ldots,128\}. The deep protocol uses L=16L=16 and 6000 steps, a 3×3\times larger budget, with dd extended to 256 in the critical region (0 unhealthy cells). The third is an L=24L=24 grid under the deep protocol with dd up to 512 (0 unhealthy). The field grids straddle the exact critical point hc/J=1h_{c}/J=1. The deep protocol continues into the paramagnet at h/J∈{4,10}h/J\in\{4,10\}, with d∈{32,64,128}d\in\{32,64,128\} (0 divergence events) and a full-parameter reference with 3 seeds per field.

The rise. At both sizes d∗d^{*} rises ∼4×{\sim}4\times across the transition (Fig. 3). The edge of the step lies inside the critical window, between h/J=1.0h/J=1.0 and 1.051.05 for L=16L=16 and between 1.051.05 and 1.11.1 for L=24L=24. Table 6 in Appendix E lists the value in every cell. The demand stays elevated through h/J=2.0h/J=2.0 and relaxes deep in the paramagnet, to d∗=64d^{*}=64 at both h/J=4h/J=4 and 1010.

The floor. The relaxation stops short of what the state needs. At h/J=10h/J=10 the product state |→⟩⊗L|{\rightarrow}\rangle^{\otimes L}, which has no parameters, is already within εrel=2.5×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}=2.5\times 10^{-3} of the exact energy, and the full-parameter reference reaches the Monte Carlo noise floor. A random 32-dimensional slice of the same network stalls at a median of 3.4×10−23.4\times 10^{-2}, which is 14 times worse than the parameter-free state. The stall is converged, since the best εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} is unchanged over the final 20% of steps in all six d=32d=32 cells at h/J∈{4,10}h/J\in\{4,10\}. The plateau shows the same split. The full-parameter reference is at its best at h/J=2.0h/J=2.0, with a median εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} of 2.5×10−32.5\times 10^{-3}, and its medians span [2.5,4.1]×10−3[2.5,4.1]\times 10^{-3} over h/J∈{1.0,1.6,2.0}h/J\in\{1.0,1.6,2.0\} with 3 seeds each and zero divergence events. At the same field, d=64d=64 subspaces still fail, with a median of 1.16×10−21.16\times 10^{-2}. d∗d^{*} therefore tracks the transition above a floor, and the floor belongs to the random slice rather than to the state.

Independence of the budget. Under a fixed step budget, a larger d∗d^{*} could mean that more directions are required, or that the same directions take longer to find. The pair of protocols separates the two. At τ=10−2\tau=10^{-2}, all 7 cells that the base and deep protocols share are unchanged under the 3×3\times larger step budget, and 0 cells shrank, so more steps do not lower d∗d^{*} (Fig. 8 in the appendix). The same control fails at tighter thresholds, which is why every d∗d^{*} claim in this paper is pinned to τ=10−2\tau=10^{-2}.

Pre-registered falsification. The L=16L=16 staircase contains an interior maximum, d∗​(1.2)=256d^{*}(1.2)=256, whose deciding median sits within +4%+4\% of the threshold. We pre-registered competing hypotheses for the L=24L=24 grid, and the hypothesis that it is an artifact was selected. At L=24L=24 no coupling requires d=256d=256, so the step is what survives (Appendix E).

Dependence on the threshold. We sweep τ\tau over [5×10−3,2×10−2][5\times 10^{-3},2\times 10^{-2}] on the existing runs. The location of the step drifts with the threshold, while its existence and confinement do not. Wherever a step exists, its edge lies inside the finite-size critical window h/J∈[0.9,1.2]h/J\in[0.9,1.2] at both sizes (Fig. 9 in the appendix).

4.4 Full-parameter training breaks at the larger lattice

The full-parameter reference broke, and the subspace configurations did not.

We train the sign-capable model with every parameter trainable, under the same SGD and minSR configuration as everywhere else, with 5 seeds per coupling. At 6×66\times 6 its final energy is bimodal across seeds (Fig. 4 in the appendix). At 4 of 7 couplings the median seed ends in a catastrophic attractor, which we call the bad basin, with E≈−11E\approx-11 to −14-14 against exact energies of −17.8-17.8 to −19.1-19.1, computed by Lanczos diagonalization in a sector of 126 million states (Appendix C). The 35 runs of this reference logged 41 divergence events and 3 aborts.

All 70 subspace runs at this size completed with zero divergence events. Their seed spread is 1.01.0–3.3×3.3\times per two-seed cell, against 1010–52×52\times across the five seeds of TC1. For a comparison at equal steps we cut every subspace run at the median step count of TC1, which is 1,000 at every coupling. The d=3072d=3072 subspace then beats the full-parameter median at exactly those four couplings, with per-coupling ratios of the median εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} of 1.61.6–4.6×4.6\times in its favour. It loses by 2.32.3–5.0×5.0\times at the three couplings where the reference median stays out of the bad basin (J2/J1=0.45J_{2}/J_{1}=0.45–0.550.55). The low-dimensional slice through θ0\theta_{0} removes the divergence but not the bad basin. When we rerun the same subspace with the minSR preconditioner of TC1, it is itself bimodal across seeds and still logs no divergence event (Sec. 3.3).

With the median seed in the bad basin, a gate that refers to the median of the reference loses its meaning, which is why Sec. 4.2 gates against 2×2\times the best reference seed. Appendix A gives both gates. We observed this failure for one optimizer configuration, plain SGD under SR or minSR. We do not claim that full-parameter NQS training is unstable in general, only that the subspace configuration is the stable one at matched optimizer and budget.

5 Discussion

5.1 Proportional allocation and small parameter blocks

PEFT methods such as LoRA give every adapted weight matrix the same rank, so a block’s budget follows its shape and not its demand (Hu et al., 2022); AdaLoRA reallocates it by importance (Zhang et al., 2023). Our dissection is a measured instance of how this can fail. The sign block holds 5.4% of the parameters, so proportional allocation gives it 28 of 512 dimensions, which leaves the error 5.9×5.9\times above an exact-sign control at the same amplitude allocation. Yet once the amplitude is well resolved, even a quarter of the sign block leaves the median error 1.24×1.24\times higher (Table 5). Low-rank adaptation with budgets set by shape gives too little to any small block whose demand exceeds its share.

5.2 Implications for NQS practice

First, subspace training is a stabilizer. We saw zero divergences across the 246 subspace runs of the sign-structure study and in every deep-protocol and L=24L=24 TFIM cell, while full-parameter training becomes bimodal at 6×66\times 6. It is worth considering wherever full-parameter VMC is fragile, within the scope stated in Appendix A. Second, d∗d^{*} is a cheap probe with a floor. Like the compute exponent of NQS scaling laws (Rende et al., 2026), it responds to the difficulty of the coupling, at roughly two orders of magnitude less compute per coupling, but its value includes what the random slice itself costs. Third, the variational-floor guard (Sec. 3.4) should be standard in any VMC that trains a latent reparameterization. It costs nothing whenever E0E_{0} or a good lower bound is known.

6 Conclusion

We brought the measurement of intrinsic dimension to variational Monte Carlo. A neural quantum state is trained inside a random subspace of its weights, SR applies without modification, and every run is scored against an exact energy. Three findings follow. Subspace training is robust under gradient noise. In our sign-structure study it never diverged, while full-parameter training with the same optimizer settings diverged repeatedly at the larger lattice. Apparent compression can be a variational bound. A network with non-negative amplitudes reaches its best energy in 8 random directions, but no such network can reach a lower energy. Once the model can represent signs, neither the sign nor the amplitude is cheap. The measured dimension tracks a phase transition, above a floor set by the random slice, so part of d∗d^{*} is a cost of the slice itself. Two measurements are the natural next steps. The first is to repeat the exact-sign control in other network families, since all our results use one. The second is to compare d∗d^{*} with compute scaling laws (Rende et al., 2026) on a shared Hamiltonian.

AI use statement

We used a large language model to polish the writing. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

Appendix A Both gates and the scope of the 6×66\times 6 failure

This appendix gives both gates, the prescription that we draw from them, and the scope of the failure of full-parameter training.

Median-referenced gates do not survive scale-up. A gate is the error that a subspace run must reach, and we set it as a multiple of the error of the full-parameter reference. With the median seed in the bad basin, a gate at 2×2\times the median of the reference inflates until it carries no information (0.31–0.57 on the final 5-seed data). The dc∗d^{*}_{c} values that it produces are artifacts of this inflation, and we discard them. We report the robust gate instead, which is 2×2\times the best reference seed. Under it dc∗d^{*}_{c} at 6×66\times 6 is right-censored (>3072>3072) at every coupling (Sec. 4.2). We state both gates, although reporting the median gate alone would have been more favorable to the subspace. The prescription is general. When the reference configuration can be multi-modal across seeds, gate against a robust statistic of the reference, or repair the reference before measuring against it.

The saturated allocation at 6×66\times 6. At 6×66\times 6 the sign block holds 2,273 of Pc=30,915P_{c}=30{,}915 parameters. The saturated allocation, d=3072d=3072, gives the sign block all of its 2,273 dimensions and the amplitude the remaining 799. Its median per coupling still stays 3.83.8–7.7×7.7\times above the best full-parameter seed, with a per-seed range of 2.42.4–8.1×8.1\times. We gate on the best seed here and ask the median to come within 2×2\times of it, which we call the robust gate (Sec. 4.4). Under this gate the demand of the sign-capable model, dc∗d^{*}_{c}, defined as the smallest dd that passes the gate, is right-censored (>3072>3072) at every coupling. This locates a failure but does not attribute it to the sign. At d=3072d=3072 the sign block is fully covered, so the residual error cannot show that the signs need more than their own 2,273 directions. At the same time the amplitude block has only 799 of 28,642 dimensions, and the two deficits cannot be separated at this allocation. We therefore report the 6×66\times 6 result as a joint failure of the saturated budget.

Scope. We demonstrated this failure of full-parameter training for one optimizer configuration. It is plain SGD under SR or minSR, the uniform choice that makes our configurations comparable. We do not claim that full-parameter NQS training is unstable in general, and better-tuned or adaptive full-parameter optimizers may well close the gap. The controlled comparison shows that at matched optimizer and budget the subspace configuration is the stable one.

Appendix B The variational-floor incident and audit

This appendix gives the four criteria of the health protocol, the incident that motivated the variational-floor guard, and the audit that followed.

An event is declared when the Monte Carlo energy estimate EE meets any of four conditions. (1) EE is not finite. (2) EE jumps upward, E>Ebest+2.0E>E_{\mathrm{best}}+2.0, where EbestE_{\mathrm{best}} is the best energy so far. (3) EE violates the variational floor, E<E0−max⁡(0.5, 5​σE)E<E_{0}-\max(0.5,\ 5\sigma_{E}), when E0E_{0} is known. (4) EE jumps downward, E<Ebest−20E<E_{\mathrm{best}}-20, when E0E_{0} is not known. Guards (3) and (4) are necessary when the objective is noisy. Milder violations of the floor would go unnoticed and look like convergence.

One run in our TFIM grid recorded a “best” energy of −4.7×107-4.7\times 10^{7}. This is far below the variational floor E0E_{0}, which no legitimate variational state can cross. Four cascading rollbacks followed, each to the poisoned state, and then an abort. Guards (1) and (2), which detect NaNs and upward jumps, saw nothing wrong, because the corruption moved the estimate downward. A milder violation of the floor would have passed for convergence without any warning. After the fix we audited all 147 base-protocol runs. Exactly one run was below the floor, the known one, so there was no silent contamination. We re-ran that seed.

Appendix C Exact reference energies at 6×66\times 6

The 6×66\times 6 reference energies are exact. We diagonalize the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Hamiltonian on the 6×66\times 6 torus in the Sz=0S^{z}=0 sector. We reduce this sector by the two lattice translations at momentum zero and by spin inversion with eigenvalue +1+1, which gives the sector of the singlet ground state. No point-group symmetry is used, so every rotation sector is included and the level crossing of the collinear regime cannot be missed. The sector holds 126,056,625 states, and the Hamiltonian has 9.3×1099.3\times 10^{9} nonzero entries. With the full point group the same lattice reduces to 15.8 million states (Schulz et al., 1996), and Richter & Schulenburg (2010) reach N=40N=40 in a sector of 430,909,650 states. A plain Lanczos recursion converges the lowest eigenvalue to 10−1210^{-12} relative in 58–118 steps. This takes about ten minutes per coupling on one CPU node, and the basis and the matrix structure are shared by all couplings.

We made three checks. At 4×44\times 4 the same code reproduces the full-space diagonalization of the main text at all seven couplings to 3×10−133\times 10^{-13}. At 4×84\times 8 it agrees with an independent implementation in QuSpin (Weinberg & Bukov, 2019) to 3×10−143\times 10^{-14}. At 6×66\times 6 the energies per site at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 and 0.550.55, −0.503810-0.503810 and −0.495178-0.495178, are the N=36N=36 values of Schulz et al. (1996).

Table 3 lists all seven energies beside DMRG torus references computed with TeNPy (Hauschild et al., 2024) (χ=4096\chi=4096). The DMRG energies are variational upper bounds. They lie above the exact energy by 1.6×10−51.6\times 10^{-5} to 1.5×10−31.5\times 10^{-3} relative, and the gap is largest in the frustrated window.

Appendix D More on the four training configurations

Reruns of the 4×44\times 4 seeds. Which attractor a seed reaches varies between reruns. At equal steps, two of the three d=8d=8 seeds in Table 2 reach the lower attractor, against one of three at d=32d=32. In a fresh 1000-step rerun of the same seeds, none of them reaches it at either dd (medians 0.717 and 0.646).

The nonlinear map on the TFIM. The base protocol also ran TC3 alongside TC2 at matched dd. On the TFIM the tanh mapping is roughly comparable to the linear subspace, and it is better at d=2d=2 and h/J=0.6h/J=0.6, where the best ε\varepsilon of TC3 is 5.6×10−25.6\times 10^{-2} against a TC2 median of 2.6×10−12.6\times 10^{-1}. Together with Sec. 4.1, this shows that the weakness of this mapping variant is specific to the frustrated system and is not caused by VMC noise as such.

Independence of the budget. Under a fixed step budget, a larger d∗d^{*} could mean that more directions are required, or that the same directions take longer to find. The pair of protocols separates the two. At τ=10−2\tau=10^{-2}, all 7 cells that the base and deep protocols share are unchanged under the 3×3\times larger step budget, and 0 cells shrank. The two cells that were censored in the base protocol resolved within the deep grid (h/J=1.1→128h/J=1.1\to 128 and 1.2→2561.2\to 256). More steps therefore do not lower d∗d^{*}, and the cells that lacked an answer needed more directions (Fig. 8). The same control fails at tighter thresholds. At 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} the outcome is mixed, and at 10−310^{-3} the one comparable cell moved 128→64128\to 64. This is why every d∗d^{*} claim in this paper is pinned to τ=10−2\tau=10^{-2}. The threshold at which d∗d^{*} is independent of the budget is thus measured and not assumed.

Pre-registered falsification. The L=16L=16 staircase contains an interior maximum, d∗​(1.2)=256d^{*}(1.2)=256. We resolved it with n=5n=5 seeds, which give a median ε\varepsilon of 0.01039 with 4/5 seeds above the threshold. The maximum is therefore confirmed at this size, but we flag it with †\dagger because the deciding median sits within +4%+4\% of the threshold. Rather than interpret it as physics, we pre-registered competing hypotheses for the L=24L=24 grid. The hypothesis that it is an artifact was selected. At L=24L=24 no coupling requires d=256d=256, and the cell that sat 4% above the threshold at L=16L=16 reads 8.0×10−38.0\times 10^{-3} at L=24L=24. The interior maximum is thus an artifact of the finite size and of the discrete threshold, and the step is what survives.

Dependence on the threshold. We sweep τ\tau over [5×10−3,2×10−2][5\times 10^{-3},2\times 10^{-2}] on the existing runs, which needs no new compute. The location of the step drifts with the threshold, while its existence and confinement do not. Wherever a step exists, its edge lies inside the finite-size critical window h/J∈[0.9,1.2]h/J\in[0.9,1.2] at both sizes. The ordered side below the window (h/J≤0.8h/J\leq 0.8) is stable in threshold and size, with d∗∈{32,64}d^{*}\in\{32,64\}. The staircase at any fixed τ\tau is a level cut of the smooth error surface εmed​(h,d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{med}}(h,d) (Fig. 9).

Appendix F Further related work

Other work counts how many directions or parameters an NQS needs with other tools. Dash et al. (2025) take the rank of the quantum geometric tensor at convergence as the number of directions a trained NQS uses, mainly for networks trained by infidelity minimization on a spin-1 chain. Park & Kastoryano (2020) find that, under SR, the converged spectrum of the quantum Fisher matrix of complex restricted Boltzmann machine states can change sharply across a phase transition. Barton et al. (2026) prune NQS of the transverse-field Ising model and the toric code by more than an order of magnitude and find that the connectivity of the sparse subnetwork, not its initialization, sets its accuracy. Their subnetworks are selected by pruning and set the removed weights to zero, while our slice is dense and drawn at random.

On the sign structure, Szabó & Castelnovo (2020) give an NQS an explicit phase ansatz and find, in frustrated antiferromagnets, low-energy states that obey the Marshall sign rule and likely keep VMC from reaching the ground state. Ou et al. (2025) train separate amplitude and phase networks on the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model, with a larger SR time step for the phase. Choo et al. (2019) benchmark a convolutional NQS on the same model, including the 6×66\times 6 lattice.
